notes: The opening joins silence and praise: it can suggest praise waiting in silence, or praise being fitting for God. The Hebrew does not explain the relationship.
Water, tracks dripping abundance, clothed hills, and singing fields form one extended picture of the land receiving God's care.
vocabulary: Atonement
The Hebrew verb kipper concerns removing or dealing with wrongdoing so the barrier it creates is overcome.
Tracks
The image is of God's passing leaving rich abundance behind.

sections.1: Come and see, come and hear

notes: The verb can describe cringing submission or feigned obedience; the enemies' inward loyalty is not asserted.
Sea and river evoke Israel's passages through water. “There” draws the worshiping community into the remembered rescue.
The Hebrew locates praise “under my tongue,” a compact image rendered here as praise ready on the tongue.
vocabulary: Ride over our heads
An image of brutal domination; the suffering is not merely embarrassment.
Burnt offerings
Sacrifices consumed on the altar; the listed animals remain distinct.

notes: The shining face echoes the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24–26. Here the desired blessing opens outward toward all nations.
The harvest has been given; the following blessing clauses can be heard as confident expectation or prayer.
vocabulary: Peoples
Distinct human communities are summoned repeatedly; the two refrains deliberately use the same words.

sections.1: God rises and leads his people

notes: “Wilderness” in verse 4 can also be understood as clouds. Verse 8's “the one of Sinai” is difficult; another reading makes Sinai itself tremble.
The heralds in verse 11 are women. The sheepfolds, silver-and-gold dove, and snow at Zalmon remain difficult images; their precise setting is uncertain.

The Hebrew's compressed language links divine chariots, Sinai, the sanctuary, ascent, captives, and received gifts. Verse 18 says “received”; later uses of the passage do not replace its wording here.

The pinned text uses a verb meaning crush or shatter. “Wash” or “dip” in some renderings reflects another interpretation or a textual adjustment. The blood and dogs' tongues are intentionally graphic.
Israel's “fountain” is rendered as its source or origin. Verse 28 follows “Your God has commanded your strength”; “Command your strength, God” requires a different reading.
The beast among the reeds and the bulls portray hostile powers without naming them. The silver clause may depict trampling silver or submission with tribute. The word rendered envoys is rare.
The word rendered prosperity in verse 6 is rare. The flock in verse 10 can mean a community or living creatures. Verse 19 leaves the object of bearing unstated; burden is supplied from the image.
vocabulary: YAH
A short form of the divine name represented elsewhere as LORD.
Shaddai
An ancient divine title, often rendered Almighty; its derivation is uncertain.
Cush
A region south of Egypt; it should not be equated automatically with the borders of a modern country.

notes: Floodwater, failing throat, unjust hatred, and repayment for an unstolen loss express the sufferer's danger. Verse 5 also acknowledges personal wrongdoing; the claims are not flattened into one another.
The bitter substance called rosh is not securely identified. The second line of verse 22 can refer to people at ease, recompense, or companions; the draft follows the first reading.
The prayer asks for severe judgment on multiple enemies. The “book of the living” evokes a register of life; the verse does not specify a developed account of the afterlife.
vocabulary: Zeal
Intense commitment to God's house, described here as consuming the speaker.
Righteousness
Here it can include a favorable or vindicating standing before God, not only personal virtue.

notes: This prayer closely parallels Psalm 40:13–17. Differences in divine names and wording are retained rather than harmonized.
vocabulary: For remembrance
A title instruction whose exact performance or ritual use is uncertain.

notes: Verse 3 retains the Hebrew image of a dwelling rock. The verb in verse 6 can suggest being brought out from the womb or sustained from birth.
Both reading notes give singular “me,” while the written forms have plural “us.” The draft follows the reading tradition and preserves the written forms in the source record.
vocabulary: Portent
An unsettling sign or object of wonder; it need not imply that observers admire the speaker.
Count
The abundance of God's saving acts exceeds the speaker's reckoning.

sections.1: Justice and peace for the king

notes: “Of Solomon” may mean by, for, or concerning Solomon. The final notice closes a collection of David's prayers; it does not erase this title or imply that no later psalm bears David's name.
Verse 5 follows “May they fear you,” not a changed text saying that the king endures. Verse 15 leaves several pronoun relationships uncertain; the receiver of life and gold is not identified afresh.
The abundant grain and flourishing city clauses are compressed. Verse 17 follows the reading tradition's flourishing name and retains the reflexive possibility of people blessing themselves by him.
The word rendered cut grass can also mean fleece. The desert dwellers of verse 9 may be understood as wilderness creatures; the submission image remains clear.
vocabulary: The River
A conventional designation for the Euphrates in this territorial picture.
Sheba and Seba
Two distinct names in the Hebrew, both retained.

notes: The draft retains “at death” and “eyes” in verses 4 and 7; other translations sometimes adjust the text. Verse 10 is obscure: “his people” and the full water they drink admit more than one explanation.
The awakening language in verse 20 is difficult. Verse 24 can suggest being received with honor, into glory, or after glory; it does not name a destination. The draft keeps that restraint.
vocabulary: Portion
An allotted share or inheritance; God himself is the poet's lasting share.
Unfaithful
The Hebrew uses a sexual-infidelity image for abandoning God.

notes: Enemy signs replace the community's signs. “Meeting places” does not by itself identify later synagogues. The damaged woodwork and burning remain concrete.

Sea monsters and many-headed Leviathan draw on ancient images of threatening waters. The recipients of Leviathan as food are difficult to identify; the Hebrew can describe desert creatures or desert dwellers as a people.
God's community is pictured as a vulnerable dove. The repeated Hebrew word hayyah connects wild creatures with the life of the afflicted.
vocabulary: Maskil
A psalm designation, perhaps related to insight or instruction; its precise musical function is uncertain.
Covenant
A binding relationship and commitment invoked as the ground for God's response.

notes: The first-person judgment speech is distinguished from the singer's praise. The final “I” may resume God's speech or voice a royal speaker; quotation marks are an editorial aid, not a Hebrew speaker label.
The final Hebrew word can be related to lifting up or read as mountains. The draft follows the raising/lowering wordplay that continues in verse 7.
The Hebrew describes wine mixed for drinking but does not name its ingredients; spices are a contextual interpretation.
vocabulary: Horn
A visible image of strength and status, drawn from an animal's horn.
Dregs
Sediment at the bottom of a wine cup; draining it pictures drinking judgment completely.

notes: Verse 4 retains the difficult “mountains of prey” rather than substituting everlasting mountains. Verse 10 literally uses girding language; some understand it as restraining the remaining wrath.
Sleep and the cutting off of spirit or breath describe defeated power. The poem does not identify a particular historical battle.
vocabulary: Salem
A poetic name associated here with Zion, Jerusalem.

notes: This difficult line can be read as grief that the Most High's hand has changed, or as an appeal recalling the years of that hand's action. The draft follows the former, leaving the subsequent remembering to make the turn.
The path through water evokes the exodus. Invisible footprints are followed by the ordinary human agency of Moses and Aaron.
vocabulary: Jeduthun
A name associated with temple music; the exact force of “according to” in the title is uncertain.
YAH
The short form of the divine name; it is retained where the Hebrew uses it.

notes: This poem teaches history through retelling, so that each generation can remember and respond. “Parable” and “riddles” frame the significance of that history rather than replacing it with a fictional story.
“Mighty ones” may refer to heavenly beings. Verse 28 retains the singular “his camp” and “his dwellings” rather than silently changing them to plural possessives.
The poem selects and orders the Egyptian plagues for its own retelling. Its sequence is not silently rearranged to match Exodus. The weather term rendered frost is rare and uncertain.

Strength and splendor in captivity evoke the captured ark. The Lord's awakening like a warrior after wine and the rearward blow are intentionally striking images, not prose descriptions of divine biology.
vocabulary: Instruction
Hebrew torah includes teaching and direction, here involving remembered history as well as commands.
Ham
An ancestral name used poetically for Egypt.
High places
Cultic sites; their name is retained rather than replaced by a general moral label.

notes: “Past wrongs” may mean former sins or the wrongs of ancestors. The plea also acknowledges the community's own sins in verse 9.
The community asks for vengeance for spilled blood and sevenfold repayment. These requests remain the sufferers' prayer; the translation does not turn them into instructions to readers.
vocabulary: Marked for death
Literally “sons of death,” describing people facing death, not their parents.

notes: The refrain's request stays the same while its address grows from “God” to “God of Armies” to “LORD, God of Armies.”

The measure of tears is uncertain. The vine's “stock” and “son” language moves into the man at God's right hand; it can evoke Israel and its representative ruler. No later identification is inserted into the verse.
vocabulary: Cherubim
Heavenly beings associated with God's throne and sanctuary, not the winged infants of later art.
The River
The Euphrates, paired with the sea as a broad territorial boundary.

sections.1: If only my people would listen

notes: The moon term is commonly understood as full moon, but the precise festival reference is uncertain. Verse 5's going out can be read as God's action against Egypt or the people's departure. “I hear” introduces an abrupt change of voice.

“Their time” in verse 15 is not explained. Verse 16 shifts from he/him to I/you. The draft identifies the collective recipient as his people, Israel, while retaining the shift of speakers and address.
vocabulary: Gittith
An uncertain musical designation, possibly related to Gath or an instrument.
Meribah
A name associated with quarreling, recalling the wilderness dispute over water.

notes: The poem calls the judged assembly “gods” and “sons of the Most High.” Interpreters differ over heavenly beings and human rulers. The translation preserves the designations and the verdict that they will die like humans.
vocabulary: Fatherless
Children without a father to protect their household interests in this ancient social setting.

sections.1: A prayer against a hostile alliance

notes: The poem names an alliance threatening Israel's existence and recalls defeats described in Judges. These ancient names are not codes for modern states.
The prayer asks both that enemies seek the LORD's name and that they perish in disgrace. Both demands remain visible.
vocabulary: Descendants of Lot
Moab and Ammon are associated with Lot in Genesis 19:30–38.
Tumbleweed
A rendering of a whirling, wind-driven object; the precise plant or image is uncertain.

sections.1: Longing for the courts of God

notes: The Hebrew speaks of highways in the heart. Baca may be a place name, a plant-related term, or wordplay suggesting weeping. The line about early rain and blessings has also been understood with pools or a teacher.
“Our shield” likely stands parallel to the anointed ruler, though it can be addressed to God. Standing at a threshold need not identify a formal doorkeeper's office.
vocabulary: Sons of Korah
A group associated with temple song; the title is retained as part of the source.
Anointed one
Someone set apart with oil, here in a royal setting; the phrase is not automatically expanded into a later identification.

notes: Past restoration grounds a fresh plea for restoration. Restoring fortunes can include return from captivity but is not limited to that situation.
Love, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace act as persons. The last clause is compressed; it may describe righteousness preparing God's route or directing footsteps along the way.
vocabulary: Peace
Hebrew shalom includes wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of fighting.

notes: Comparison “among the gods” and the claim “you alone are God” both occur. Neither is removed to simplify the poem's language.
The mercy formula recalls Exodus 34:6. Calling oneself the son of God's servant woman expresses a deeply rooted dependent relationship, retaining the mother's part in it.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead; it is not automatically the later idea of a place of final punishment.

notes: Rahab here is a poetic name for Egypt, not the woman in Joshua. The nations and the repeated birth notices portray belonging to Zion; the precise force of “there” in verse 4 remains debated.
The final line joins performers and springs. The second group may be dancers or pipe players; springs remain the image for the speaker's source of life.
The Hebrew opens with “his foundation.” The city is supplied from the following reference to Zion so readers can follow the subject.
vocabulary: Cush
A region south of Egypt, kept distinct from modern national boundaries.

notes: Mahalath Leannoth and maskil are uncertain musical or performance designations. The title associates the psalm with both the sons of Korah and Heman the Ezrahite.

Verse 5 can picture release or separation among the dead. The final verb of verse 15 is rare and uncertain. Verse 18 ends in darkness; it may describe darkness as the only companion or companions lost in darkness. No resolution is added.
vocabulary: Shades
Hebrew rephaim here refers to the dead in the underworld.
Abaddon
A term for destruction or the realm of destruction, paired with the grave.

sections.1: The covenant and the fallen crown

notes: The heavenly council, sons of gods, and defeated Rahab belong to the poem's ancient cosmic imagery. Rahab here is a threatening sea figure, unlike its use for Egypt in Psalm 87.
The pinned Hebrew has plural “faithful ones.” The verb in verse 22 can concern extracting tribute or outwitting; the draft follows the oppressive-creditor sense.
“Firstborn” is a rank bestowed on the king. The faithful heavenly witness in verse 37 can be the moon or a further witness alongside it.

The complaint deliberately confronts the preceding promise with apparent covenant repudiation. The term rendered splendor in verse 44 and the compressed description of carrying the peoples' taunts in verse 50 are uncertain.
This doxology closes the third collection of Psalms. It does not supply an answer to every question in the lament.
vocabulary: YAH
The short form of the divine name, occurring alongside LORD in this verse.
Horn
An animal-derived image of strength and elevated status.

sections.1: Teach us to count our days

notes: The word rendered dust suggests crushed material. Flooding away, sleep, and grass overlap as pictures of brief human life.
Seventy and eighty are the poem's lifespan figures, not a promise that each person will reach either age. Counting days means reckoning with their limits.
vocabulary: Dwelling place
The image presents God as a lasting home across generations.

notes: The psalm changes speakers and addressees. Verse 2 retains “I say”; verse 9 retains “my refuge” followed by “your dwelling.” The final three verses speak in God's first person.
The poem voices strong assurances of protection and also promises God's presence “in distress.” Both are retained without turning the poetry into a formula for testing danger.
vocabulary: Shaddai
An ancient divine title, traditionally Almighty, whose derivation is uncertain.
Protective wall; serpent
Soherah is an uncommon defense term, also rendered buckler. Tannin can denote a large serpent or monster; the animal imagery is retained.

notes: The oil verb is difficult and can suggest anointing or refreshing. Verse 11 does not state exactly what the eyes see and ears hear; the draft does not add delight in an enemy's death.
The wicked's quick-growing grass contrasts with enduring, fruitful palm and cedar trees, including fruit in old age.
vocabulary: Sabbath
The seventh-day rest; this is the only psalm whose Hebrew title names the Sabbath day.

notes: Royal clothing, earth's stability, and rising waters form a poetic portrayal of divine rule. The ancient images are not rewritten as modern scientific claims.
vocabulary: Testimonies
God's trustworthy declarations or authoritative directions.

notes: The poem names the killing of vulnerable people and destructive rule operating through law. The indictment concerns actual injustice, without adding a modern partisan target.
vocabulary: Vengeance
The requested divine reckoning with wrong; its force is retained alongside the specific injuries in the psalm.
YAH
The short divine name used in both the enemies' speech and the poet's prayer.

notes: The invitation to worship turns into a warning in God's voice. The final Hebrew oath has the force of a firm denial: they will not enter his rest.
vocabulary: Meribah and Massah
Names associated with quarreling and testing in Israel's wilderness story.

sections.1: A new song for all the earth

notes: “Gods” and “worthless idols” echo each other's sounds in Hebrew. “Holy splendor” may describe divine holiness or the worshipers' sacred attire; the main text does not force the distinction.
vocabulary: Ascribe
Acknowledge glory and strength as belonging to God; the worshipers do not create those qualities.

sections.1: The earth rejoices at its king

notes: The command addresses “all you gods,” not a substituted term for angels. Verse 10 retains the command to those who love the LORD. Verse 11 follows “light is sown,” rather than a variant reading in which light dawns.
vocabulary: Daughters of Judah
A poetic way of speaking of Judah's towns and their communities.

notes: The poem holds Israel's particular experience and the nations' witness together. Its ending resembles Psalm 96 but has its own wording, retained here.
vocabulary: Trumpets and ram's horn
Distinct instruments: metal trumpets and an animal horn.

notes: Verse 4 compresses royal strength and love of justice. Moses and Aaron are both included among priests. Forgiveness and vengeance for deeds stand together in verse 8; neither is omitted.
vocabulary: Footstool
A royal image for the place beneath God's throne, associated with his earthly sanctuary.

notes: The reading tradition has “we belong to him.” The written text has “and not we,” often understood as “not we ourselves.” The draft follows the reading tradition, while the source record preserves both.
vocabulary: Thanksgiving
The title may also be associated with a thanksgiving offering; the psalm invites grateful worship.

notes: The question about God's coming interrupts a ruler's pledges. The promises to destroy wrongdoers remain severe royal language, not merely a vow to avoid bad habits.
vocabulary: Integrity
A whole, undivided commitment, here applied to private conduct and the choice of those who serve the ruler.

notes: The terms rendered embers and desert owl are uncertain; exact bird species cannot be established. Using the sufferer's name in curses means invoking a fate like his.
The reading tradition has “my strength,” while the written form has “his strength.” The Hebrew's personal complaint is retained; later quotations do not replace its speaker structure.
vocabulary: YAH
The short form of the divine name.
Marked for death
Literally “sons of death,” people facing death who are pictured here as captives.

sections.1: Bless the LORD, my whole being

notes: The speaker addresses the whole self, grammatically feminine in Hebrew, not a separate female person. The word rendered life in verse 5 is difficult; alternatives include desire, years, or adornment.
The praise says God heals all diseases and also dwells on human frailty and mortality. Both claims are retained in the poem's own sequence.
vocabulary: Redeems
Recovers or frees a life from the pit; the verb draws on the action of a redeemer.

sections.1: The earth is full of your creatures

notes: Verse 4 may also be read “makes his messengers winds.” Verse 8 may describe mountains rising and valleys sinking, or waters going over mountains and down valleys. The draft follows the first reading in each case.
Some tree identifications are uncertain. Hyraxes are small rock-dwelling mammals, not rabbits. Leviathan is playful here; the last phrase may mean that it plays in the sea or that God plays with it.
Breath and spirit share the Hebrew word ruach; the draft keeps breath across death and renewed creation. The closing wish says sinners, not merely sins, should vanish, and its force is retained.
vocabulary: Upper rooms
An ancient architectural image of God's dwelling above the waters.
Praise YAH
Hebrew hallelu-yah, joining a plural call to praise with the short divine name.
